::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## The end-of-course project goal

Your team answers a predictive question with a public data set, in R and/or Python,
with a focus on reproducible and trustworthy workflows.
**By the end of the course**, your single Quarto document will have become a project with:

-   well-documented, modular scripts in R and/or Python
-   a pipeline automated with GNU Make
-   a reproducible Quarto report
-   a Docker container for the computational environment
-   a GitHub repository for collaboration and sharing
:::

## Milestone 2 summary

This milestone is about moving your project into a [container]{.term tabindex="0" data-tip="A container is a running copy of a Docker image: an isolated computer inside your computer, with the exact software and packages your project needs. Everyone who runs it gets the same environment, whatever their own laptop has installed."}.

- [ ] Run your project's environment in a Docker container, and **work in it from now on**
- [ ] Build the [image]{.term tabindex="0" data-tip="A Docker image is a saved snapshot of a computer setup: an operating system, software and packages, ready to run. A container is one running copy of it. Your Dockerfile is the recipe for your project's image."} on [GitHub Actions]{.term tabindex="0" data-tip="GitHub Actions runs commands for you on a fresh computer at GitHub when something happens in your repository, such as a push. You write the commands in a workflow file (a .yml file in .github/workflows/). Here it builds your image and uploads it to Docker Hub."} for [Intel/AMD and ARM]{.term tabindex="0" data-tip="These are the two main kinds of computer processor. Most Windows laptops and servers use Intel/AMD chips (linux/amd64), while Macs with Apple silicon (M1 and later) use ARM chips (linux/arm64). An image built for one kind runs slowly or not at all on the other, so you build for both."}, and publish it on [Docker Hub]{.term tabindex="0" data-tip="Docker Hub is a website that stores Docker images, the way GitHub stores code. Anyone can download a public image from it. Here your team publishes its image there, so everyone downloads the same one instead of building their own."}
- [ ] Update your `README` and `CONTRIBUTING.md` so they use the container
- [ ] Publish your report on [GitHub Pages]{.term tabindex="0" data-tip="GitHub Pages is a free GitHub service that turns files in a repository into a public website. Here it shows your rendered report at a web address, so anyone can read it without cloning your repository."}

We give you the [`Dockerfile`](#dockerfile), the [workflow file](#workflow-file) and [`docker-compose.yml`]{.term tabindex="0" data-tip="Docker Compose starts a container from settings written in a docker-compose.yml file (which image, which ports, which folders to share), so you don't have to type a long docker run command. Here everyone on the team starts the same container with one short command."} ([see below](#compose-file)).
They are adapted from [docker-uv-renv](https://github.com/chendaniely/docker-uv-renv).

::: callout-important

If you lost points for something in Milestone 1, we won't take points off again for it in Milestone 2.
That would be unfair: you may not get your Milestone 1 grades back before Milestone 2 is due.
Still fix it once you get the feedback: later milestones build on this work, and in Milestone 4 you can fix the mistakes you made in previous milestones.

## Readings for this milestone

-   [Python and R in one image](https://ubc-dsci.github.io/reproducible-and-trustworthy-workflows-for-data-science/lectures/containers-uv-renv.html): what each line of the `Dockerfile` does
-   [uv in a container](https://ubc-dsci.github.io/reproducible-and-trustworthy-workflows-for-data-science/lectures/containers-uv.html) and [renv in a container](https://ubc-dsci.github.io/reproducible-and-trustworthy-workflows-for-data-science/lectures/containers-renv.html): adding a package to your image
-   [renv: declaring packages in `DESCRIPTION`](https://ubc-dsci.github.io/reproducible-and-trustworthy-workflows-for-data-science/lectures/virtual-environments-r-renv-description.html): pinning R package versions
-   [Docker Compose](https://ubc-dsci.github.io/reproducible-and-trustworthy-workflows-for-data-science/lectures/containers-docker-compose.html): starting the container with one command
-   [Working in a container over ssh with Positron](https://ubc-dsci.github.io/reproducible-and-trustworthy-workflows-for-data-science/lectures/containers-ssh-positron.html): editing code inside the container
-   [Building images for several platforms](https://ubc-dsci.github.io/reproducible-and-trustworthy-workflows-for-data-science/lectures/containers-platforms.html): why the workflow builds for two kinds of computer
-   [Introduction to Quarto and GitHub Pages](https://ubc-mds.github.io/DSCI_521_platforms-dsci_book/lectures/quarto-github-pages.html) (DSCI 521): publishing the report in part 3
:::

### 1. Put your environment in a container

1.  **Add the `Dockerfile`.**
    Copy the version for your project's language(s) [below](#dockerfile) into a file named `Dockerfile` in the root of your repository.
    If you use R, change `4.6.2` on the `FROM` line to the R version in your `renv.lock`.
    Always keep a version tag on the `FROM` line, never `latest`.

2.  **Check your environment files.**
    The image installs your packages from your [lock files]{.term tabindex="0" data-tip="A lock file (uv.lock for uv, renv.lock for renv) is generated by your environment manager. It records the exact version of every package your project uses, including the packages they depend on, so the environment can be rebuilt exactly."},
    so these must be in your repository and agree with each other:

    -   **Python (uv):** `pyproject.toml` with every package [pinned]{.term tabindex="0" data-tip="Pinning means recording one exact version of a package (e.g. pandas==2.2.3), instead of whatever is newest. Everyone who installs your project then gets the same version, so the code behaves the same."} with `==` (not `>=`), `uv.lock` and `.python-version`.
        It **must list `ipykernel`, `nbclient` and `pyyaml`** (Quarto needs them to run the Python code in your report).
    -   **R (renv):** `DESCRIPTION` with every package pinned with `(== x.y.z)`, `renv.lock`, `.Rprofile` and `renv/`.
        `DESCRIPTION` is required, and it **must list `knitr` and `rmarkdown`**
        (Quarto needs them to run the R code in your report).

3.  **Test the build on your computer** before you push:
    `docker build --tag my-project .` (as in Individual Assignment 2).
    Fixing errors here is much faster than on GitHub Actions.

4.  **Build and publish the image with GitHub Actions.**

    -   One team member sets up Docker Hub and the GitHub [secrets]{.term tabindex="0" data-tip="A repository secret is a password or token saved in your GitHub repository's settings. Workflows can use it, but nobody can read it back, and it never shows up in your code or logs. Here the two secrets let the workflow log in to Docker Hub as your team."} (see [below](#docker-hub-secrets)).
    -   Copy the [workflow below](#workflow-file) into `.github/workflows/publish-dockerhub.yml`, then commit and push.
        You don't need to change anything in it.
    -   It builds for `linux/amd64` (Intel/AMD) and `linux/arm64` (ARM, such as Apple silicon Macs),
        and publishes them under two [tags]{.term tabindex="0" data-tip="A tag is a label on a Docker image, written after a colon (e.g. python:3.14-slim). One image can have several tags. Here latest always points to your newest image, and the sha- tag names the commit that built it."}: `latest` and `sha-` plus 7 characters of the commit ID.
    -   Check that the run succeeds and that your image's tag on Docker Hub lists **both** platforms.
    -   **Don't turn on [branch protection]{.term tabindex="0" data-tip="Branch protection is a GitHub setting (Settings > Branches or Rules) that puts rules on a branch, such as: nobody may push to main directly, every change must come through a reviewed pull request. Here the workflow pushes the new image tag straight to your branch, including main, so those rules would block it and the run would fail."} for `main`**:
        the workflow commits the new image tag straight to your branches, and branch protection would block it.

5.  **Add `docker-compose.yml`.**

    -   Copy the [file below](#compose-file) into the root of your repository.
    -   Change its `image:` line to your image, pinned to the [commit-SHA tag]{.term tabindex="0" data-tip="Every Git commit has a unique ID called its SHA (e.g. 1a2b3c4). Your workflow tags each image it pushes with the start of the SHA of the commit that built it, so the tag always points to that one exact image. The latest tag, by contrast, changes every time you publish."} your workflow pushed, not `latest`
        (for example, `image: yourname/your-github-repo-name:sha-1a2b3c4`, all in lowercase).
        You only do this once: after that, the workflow updates the tag for you.
    -   Keep the [service name]{.term tabindex="0" data-tip="In Docker Compose, a service is one container it manages, named under services: in docker-compose.yml. Commands such as docker compose run use that name to say which container you mean. Here the name is analysis-env."} `analysis-env`, so the [commands in part 2](#readme-steps) work as written.

6.  **Work in the container from now on**, with Positron over [ssh]{.term tabindex="0" data-tip="ssh (secure shell) lets you log in to another computer and work on it from your own. Here the other computer is your container: Positron connects to it over ssh, so your code runs with the container's software while your files stay in your project folder."}
    Follow the [step-by-step guide below](#positron-ssh) the first time.
    To add a package:

    -   On a branch, add it with uv or renv, commit the changed files together and push.
    -   GitHub Actions publishes a new image and commits its tag to `docker-compose.yml` on that branch.
    -   Run `git pull` and `docker compose pull`, then merge the branch in a pull request.
    -   The merge builds the image once more and commits a new tag to `main`.
        When that run finishes, everyone runs `git pull` on `main` and `docker compose pull` again.

::: {#dockerfile .callout-tip collapse="true"}
## The `Dockerfile` (step 1)

Pick the tab for your project. All three start the ssh server, so you can work in the container with Positron.

::: panel-tabset
## Python only

```{.dockerfile filename="Dockerfile"}
# Adapted from docker-uv-renv by Daniel Chen (MIT License)
# https://github.com/chendaniely/docker-uv-renv

# Start from Ubuntu Linux (this image also has R, which you can ignore).
FROM rocker/r-ver:4.6.2

# Install the programs the project needs:
# curl downloads files, git/less/nano let you work in a terminal,
# make runs a Makefile, openssh-server lets Positron connect over ssh
RUN apt-get update && apt-get install --yes \
    curl \
    git \
    less \
    make \
    nano \
    openssh-server

# Install Quarto (it comes with Typst for PDFs, so no LaTeX).
# dpkg --print-architecture gives amd64 or arm64, to match the computer.
RUN curl --location --output quarto.deb \
    https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/releases/download/v1.11.9/quarto-1.11.9-linux-$(dpkg --print-architecture).deb \
  && apt-get install --yes ./quarto.deb \
  && rm quarto.deb

# Copy the uv program into the image (0.13.7 pins uv's version)
COPY --from=ghcr.io/astral-sh/uv:0.13.7 /uv /uvx /usr/local/bin/

# Your project folder is mounted at /workspace,
# so the packages go in /opt instead
WORKDIR /workspace

# Python packages (uv) go in /opt/venv
ENV UV_PROJECT_ENVIRONMENT=/opt/venv
# ssh logins don't see ENV, only /etc/environment
RUN echo "UV_PROJECT_ENVIRONMENT=$UV_PROJECT_ENVIRONMENT" >> /etc/environment
COPY pyproject.toml uv.lock .python-version ./
# --locked: stop if uv.lock doesn't match pyproject.toml
RUN uv sync --locked

# On a Linux laptop, remove the # from the next line.
# (sshd wants root to own the key file, but on Linux the mounted one is yours.)
# RUN echo "StrictModes no" > /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/container.conf

# Start the ssh server when the container starts.
# -D keeps it in the foreground, so the container keeps running.
CMD ["/usr/sbin/sshd", "-D"]
```

## R only

```{.dockerfile filename="Dockerfile"}
# Adapted from docker-uv-renv by Daniel Chen (MIT License)
# https://github.com/chendaniely/docker-uv-renv

# Start from Ubuntu Linux with R installed.
# Change 4.6.2 to the R version in your renv.lock.
FROM rocker/r-ver:4.6.2

# Install the programs the project needs:
# curl downloads files, git/less/nano let you work in a terminal,
# make runs a Makefile, openssh-server lets Positron connect over ssh,
# libuv1-dev is needed by the R package fs
RUN apt-get update && apt-get install --yes \
    curl \
    git \
    less \
    libuv1-dev \
    make \
    nano \
    openssh-server

# Install Quarto (it comes with Typst for PDFs, so no LaTeX).
# dpkg --print-architecture gives amd64 or arm64, to match the computer.
RUN curl --location --output quarto.deb \
    https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/releases/download/v1.11.9/quarto-1.11.9-linux-$(dpkg --print-architecture).deb \
  && apt-get install --yes ./quarto.deb \
  && rm quarto.deb

# Your project folder is mounted at /workspace,
# so the packages go in /opt instead
WORKDIR /workspace

# R packages (renv) go in /opt/renv/library
RUN echo "RENV_PATHS_LIBRARY=/opt/renv/library" >> /usr/local/lib/R/etc/Renviron.site
COPY renv.lock .Rprofile ./
COPY renv/activate.R renv/
RUN Rscript -e "renv::restore()"

# On a Linux laptop, remove the # from the next line.
# (sshd wants root to own the key file, but on Linux the mounted one is yours.)
# RUN echo "StrictModes no" > /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/container.conf

# Start the ssh server when the container starts.
# -D keeps it in the foreground, so the container keeps running.
CMD ["/usr/sbin/sshd", "-D"]
```

With R only, you render with `quarto render` instead of `uv run quarto render`.

```{.dockerfile filename="Dockerfile"}
# Adapted from docker-uv-renv by Daniel Chen (MIT License)
# https://github.com/chendaniely/docker-uv-renv

# Start from Ubuntu Linux with R installed.
# Change 4.6.2 to the R version in your renv.lock.
FROM rocker/r-ver:4.6.2

# Install the programs the project needs:
# curl downloads files, git/less/nano let you work in a terminal,
# make runs a Makefile, openssh-server lets Positron connect over ssh,
# libuv1-dev is needed by the R package fs
RUN apt-get update && apt-get install --yes \
    curl \
    git \
    less \
    libuv1-dev \
    make \
    nano \
    openssh-server

# Install Quarto (it comes with Typst for PDFs, so no LaTeX).
# dpkg --print-architecture gives amd64 or arm64, to match the computer.
RUN curl --location --output quarto.deb \
    https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/releases/download/v1.11.9/quarto-1.11.9-linux-$(dpkg --print-architecture).deb \
  && apt-get install --yes ./quarto.deb \
  && rm quarto.deb

# Copy the uv program into the image (0.13.7 pins uv's version)
COPY --from=ghcr.io/astral-sh/uv:0.13.7 /uv /uvx /usr/local/bin/

# Your project folder is mounted at /workspace,
# so the packages go in /opt instead
WORKDIR /workspace

# ---- Python packages (uv), in /opt/venv ----
ENV UV_PROJECT_ENVIRONMENT=/opt/venv
# ssh logins don't see ENV, only /etc/environment
RUN echo "UV_PROJECT_ENVIRONMENT=$UV_PROJECT_ENVIRONMENT" >> /etc/environment
COPY pyproject.toml uv.lock .python-version ./
# --locked: stop if uv.lock doesn't match pyproject.toml
RUN uv sync --locked

# ---- R packages (renv), in /opt/renv/library ----
RUN echo "RENV_PATHS_LIBRARY=/opt/renv/library" >> /usr/local/lib/R/etc/Renviron.site
COPY renv.lock .Rprofile ./
COPY renv/activate.R renv/
RUN Rscript -e "renv::restore()"

# On a Linux laptop, remove the # from the next line.
# (sshd wants root to own the key file, but on Linux the mounted one is yours.)
# RUN echo "StrictModes no" > /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/container.conf

# Start the ssh server when the container starts.
# -D keeps it in the foreground, so the container keeps running.
CMD ["/usr/sbin/sshd", "-D"]
```

::: {#docker-hub-secrets .callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Setting up Docker Hub and the GitHub secrets (step 4)

One team member:

1.  Creates a **public** Docker Hub repository with the **same name as your GitHub repository, in lowercase**
    (e.g. GitHub `Wine_Quality_Predictor` becomes Docker Hub `wine_quality_predictor`).
2.  Creates a Docker Hub [access token](https://docs.docker.com/security/access-tokens/) with Read & Write permissions.
3.  Adds two [repository secrets](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/how-tos/write-workflows/choose-what-workflows-do/use-secrets)
    to your GitHub repository (Settings \> Secrets and variables \> Actions \> New repository secret):
    `DOCKER_USERNAME` (the Docker Hub username)
    and `DOCKER_PASSWORD` (the access token, **not** the Docker Hub password).
:::

::: {#workflow-file .callout-tip collapse="true"}
## The workflow file (step 4)

Job 1 runs the same `docker build` and `docker push` as Individual Assignment 2, on an Intel/AMD and an ARM computer at the same time.
Job 2 puts the two images under one tag.
Job 3 writes that new tag into your `docker-compose.yml` and commits it to the branch you pushed.
You don't need to change anything: the workflow names your image from the `DOCKER_USERNAME` secret and your GitHub repository's name.

```{.yaml filename=".github/workflows/publish-dockerhub.yml"}
# Builds the image from your Dockerfile for Intel/AMD and ARM computers,
# and publishes it on Docker Hub.
# Save this file as .github/workflows/publish-dockerhub.yml

name: Publish image to Docker Hub

# When the workflow runs
on:
  # by hand: Actions tab > Publish image to Docker Hub > Run workflow
  workflow_dispatch:
  # on its own: when a push changes one of these files
  push:
    # only branch pushes, not tags: a release creates a tag, and GitHub
    # ignores the paths filter for tag pushes, so it would run every release
    branches:
      - '**'
    paths:
      - Dockerfile
      - pyproject.toml
      - uv.lock
      - .python-version
      - renv.lock
      - .Rprofile
      - renv/activate.R
      - .github/workflows/publish-dockerhub.yml

env:
  # Your image: your Docker Hub username / this GitHub repository's name.
  # Nothing to change here.
  IMAGE_NAME: ${{ secrets.DOCKER_USERNAME }}/${{ github.event.repository.name }}

jobs:
  # Job 1: build the image on two computers at the same time,
  # one Intel/AMD and one ARM, and push one tag from each
  build:
    strategy:
      matrix:
        include:
          - runner: ubuntu-latest     # Intel/AMD
            arch: amd64
          - runner: ubuntu-24.04-arm  # ARM
            arch: arm64
    runs-on: ${{ matrix.runner }}
    steps:
      # 1. Docker image names must be lowercase, so save a lowercase copy as IMAGE
      - name: Make the image name lowercase
        run: echo "IMAGE=$(echo "$IMAGE_NAME" | tr '[:upper:]' '[:lower:]')" >> "$GITHUB_ENV"

      # 2. Copy your repository onto the computer
      - name: Check out the repository
        uses: actions/checkout@v7

      # 3. Log in to Docker Hub with your two repository secrets
      - name: Log in to Docker Hub
        uses: docker/login-action@v4
        with:
          username: ${{ secrets.DOCKER_USERNAME }}
          password: ${{ secrets.DOCKER_PASSWORD }}

      # 4. Build the image for this computer, tagged for example sha-1a2b3c4-arm64
      #    (sha- plus the first 7 characters of the commit ID, plus the chip)
      - name: Build the image
        run: docker build --tag "$IMAGE:sha-${GITHUB_SHA::7}-${{ matrix.arch }}" .

      # 5. Upload it to Docker Hub
      - name: Push the image
        run: docker push "$IMAGE:sha-${GITHUB_SHA::7}-${{ matrix.arch }}"

  # Job 2: after both builds finish, put the two images under one tag,
  # so each computer downloads the one for its chip
  combine:
    needs: build
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      # Docker image names must be lowercase, so save a lowercase copy as IMAGE
      - name: Make the image name lowercase
        run: echo "IMAGE=$(echo "$IMAGE_NAME" | tr '[:upper:]' '[:lower:]')" >> "$GITHUB_ENV"

      - name: Log in to Docker Hub
        uses: docker/login-action@v4
        with:
          username: ${{ secrets.DOCKER_USERNAME }}
          password: ${{ secrets.DOCKER_PASSWORD }}

      # Make the tags latest and sha-1a2b3c4, each holding both images
      - name: Combine the two images under one tag
        run: |
          docker buildx imagetools create \
            --tag "$IMAGE:latest" \
            --tag "$IMAGE:sha-${GITHUB_SHA::7}" \
            "$IMAGE:sha-${GITHUB_SHA::7}-amd64" \
            "$IMAGE:sha-${GITHUB_SHA::7}-arm64"

  # Job 3: write the new tag into docker-compose.yml and commit it
  # to the branch you pushed, so your team only has to git pull
  update-compose:
    needs: combine
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    # lets this job push a commit to your repository
    permissions:
      contents: write
    steps:
      - name: Check out the repository
        uses: actions/checkout@v7

      # Replace the image: line, e.g. image: yourname/your-repo:sha-1a2b3c4
      # (skipped if you have no docker-compose.yml yet)
      - name: Put the new tag in docker-compose.yml
        if: hashFiles('docker-compose.yml') != ''
        run: |
          IMAGE=$(echo "$IMAGE_NAME" | tr '[:upper:]' '[:lower:]')
          sed -i "s|^\( *image:\).*|\1 $IMAGE:sha-${GITHUB_SHA::7}|" docker-compose.yml

      # Commit and push the change (does nothing if the file didn't change)
      - name: Commit and push docker-compose.yml
        if: hashFiles('docker-compose.yml') != ''
        run: |
          git config user.name "github-actions[bot]"
          git config user.email "41898282+github-actions[bot]@users.noreply.github.com"
          git add docker-compose.yml
          git diff --cached --quiet && exit 0
          git commit -m "Use image tag sha-${GITHUB_SHA::7} in docker-compose.yml"
          git pull --rebase
          git push
```

It runs on its own when a push changes the `Dockerfile`, a file the `Dockerfile` copies into the image, or the workflow file.
To run it by hand: **Actions** tab \> **Publish image to Docker Hub** \> **Run workflow**.
On Docker Hub you will see four tags: `latest`, `sha-1a2b3c4`, and the two halves `sha-1a2b3c4-amd64` and `sha-1a2b3c4-arm64`.
Job 3 puts the one without `-amd64` or `-arm64` in `docker-compose.yml` for you.
Then run **`git pull`** to get that commit, and `docker compose pull` to download the new image.
:::

::: {#compose-file .callout-tip collapse="true"}
## The `docker-compose.yml` file (step 5)

Change only the `image:` line.

```{.yaml filename="docker-compose.yml"}
# Adapted from docker-uv-renv by Daniel Chen (MIT License)
# https://github.com/chendaniely/docker-uv-renv

services:
  # the service name: `docker compose run analysis-env ...` uses it
  analysis-env:
    # CHANGE THIS LINE once: your Docker Hub username / your GitHub repository's
    # name in lowercase, with the sha- tag your workflow pushed (not latest).
    # After that, the workflow updates the tag for you.
    image: your-docker-hub-username/your-github-repo-name:sha-1a2b3c4
    ports:
      # 2222 on your computer, 22 (ssh) in the container
      - "2222:22"
    volumes:
      # your project folder, at /workspace in the container
      - .:/workspace
      # your ssh public key, so you can log in (ro: read-only)
      - ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub:/root/.ssh/authorized_keys:ro
      # your Git name and email, so your commits in the container count as yours
      - ~/.gitconfig:/root/.gitconfig:ro
```

There is no `build: .` line: everyone downloads the image your workflow published, instead of building their own.
:::

::: {#positron-ssh .callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Connect Positron to the container over ssh, step by step (step 6)

Your `CONTRIBUTING.md` walks your teammates through these same steps (see [part 2](#readme-steps)).

**Once, before your first connection:**

1.  Install [Positron](https://positron.posit.co/download.html) on your computer.
    Its **Remote SSH** feature, which connects to the container, comes built in, so you don't need an extension.
2.  Make an ssh key if you don't have one. In a terminal on your computer, run `ssh-keygen -t ed25519` and press Enter at each question.
    Check that `~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub` now exists.
3.  Check that Git knows who you are on your computer: `git config --global user.email` should print the email of your GitHub account.
    If it prints nothing, set it with `git config --global user.name "Your Name"` and `git config --global user.email "you@example.com"`.
    `docker-compose.yml` shares this with the container, so your commits there count as yours.
4.  Download the image: in your project folder, run `docker compose pull`.

**Each time you work on the project:**

1.  In a terminal, in your project folder, start the container in the background:

    ```bash
    docker compose up -d
    ```

    `docker compose ps` should list `analysis-env` as running.
2.  In Positron, open the Command Palette (`Cmd+Shift+P` on Mac, `Ctrl+Shift+P` on Windows).
3.  Type and run **Remote SSH: Show Remote Menu**, then pick **Connect to Host**.
4.  Type `root@localhost:2222` and press Enter.
    A new Positron window opens.
    -   If it asks for the platform of the remote host, pick **Linux**.
    -   If it asks whether you trust the host (a "fingerprint"), click **Continue**.
    -   The first time, Positron installs its server inside the container. This takes a few minutes (e.g., took > 5 minutes on Sky's computer).
5.  **Open your project folder.** You are connected now (the bottom left corner shows `SSH: localhost:2222`),
    but the Explorer says **No folder opened**, and a terminal starts in `/root`, the container's home folder, which has no project files.
    That is normal.
    -   Click **Open Folder** in the Explorer. A path box appears at the top of the window.
    -   Delete what is in it, type `/workspace`, and press Enter (or click **OK**, you may need to click "ok" a few times before this works).
    -   The window reloads. The Explorer now shows **WORKSPACE \[SSH: LOCALHOST:2222\]** with your project files.
        A file you change here changes on your computer too.
6.  **Pick the interpreter.** Positron may start a different Python than your project's, so check this every time.
    Click the interpreter button at the top right of the window (it shows a Python or R version).
    The menu that opens, **Running Interpreter Sessions**, only lists sessions that are already running
    (such as `/usr/bin/python3`, the container's system Python: not this one). Click **New Console Session...**, then:
    -   **Python:** pick the one named **Python 3.x (uv: your-project-name)** with the path `/opt/venv/bin/python`,
        the environment built from your `uv.lock`. The top right button then shows that name.
        If it isn't in the list, open the Command Palette, run **Python: Select Interpreter**, choose **Enter interpreter path...** and type `/opt/venv/bin/python`.
        Don't pick `/workspace/.venv`: that is the environment from your own computer, and it doesn't run in the container.
    -   **R:** pick the R version in the list. It already uses the packages from your `renv.lock`.
    -   To check, run `import sys; print(sys.executable)` in the Console. It should print `/opt/venv/bin/python`.
7.  Work as usual. The Terminal, Console and **Render** button all run inside the container.
8.  When you are done, close the Positron window, then stop the container in a terminal on your computer:

    ```bash
    docker compose down
    ```

**If it doesn't connect:**

-   **`~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub` is a folder:** Docker made it because the key didn't exist yet.
    Run `docker compose down`, delete that folder, make the key (step 2 above), and start again.
-   **`~/.gitconfig` is a folder, or Git in the container doesn't know your name:** the same thing happened with your Git settings.
    Run `docker compose down`, delete that folder, set your name and email (step 3 above), and start again.
-   **GitHub asks you to sign in when you push from the container:** sign in once in the browser window Positron opens. Positron remembers it.
-   **It asks for a password:** the container can't see your key.
    Check that your key is named `id_ed25519.pub`, or change the key path in `docker-compose.yml`.
-   **"Remote host identification has changed":** you are using a new image. Run `ssh-keygen -R "[localhost]:2222"`, then connect again.
-   **Linux laptops:** ssh refuses the key because the file belongs to you, not `root`.
    Remove the `#` from the `StrictModes no` line in the `Dockerfile` and push, so the workflow publishes a fixed image.
-   **Port 2222 is already in use:** change the first `2222` in `docker-compose.yml` to another number (e.g. `2223`), and connect to that port instead.

More detail: [Working in a container over ssh with Positron](https://ubc-dsci.github.io/reproducible-and-trustworthy-workflows-for-data-science/lectures/containers-ssh-positron.html).
:::

### 2. Update your `README` and `CONTRIBUTING.md` {#readme-steps}

-   **`README`**: for someone who wants to **run** your analysis.
-   **`CONTRIBUTING.md`**: for a teammate or contributor who wants to **change** it.

Keep each set of steps in its own file.

**Your `README`:** use the [example `README.md`](https://github.com/UBC-MDS/DSCI_522_project-template-breast-cancer-predictor/blob/1.0.0/README.md) as your template.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## What your `README` must include

In this order:

- [ ] Make an [ssh key]{.term tabindex="0" data-tip="An ssh key is a pair of files that proves who you are without a password: a private key you keep secret (~/.ssh/id_ed25519) and a public key you can share (~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub). Here docker-compose.yml puts your public key in the container, so ssh lets you in."} if you don't have one: `ssh-keygen -t ed25519`, pressing Enter at each question.
      (Without it, Docker makes a *folder* named `~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub`,
      and ssh into the container fails until you delete that folder and make the key.)
- [ ] Download the image: `docker compose pull`.
- [ ] Render the report in the container:
    -   Python, or Python and R: `docker compose run --rm analysis-env uv run quarto render`
    -   R only: `docker compose run --rm analysis-env quarto render`
    -   Add your report's path after `quarto render` if your project has no `_quarto.yml` that lists it.
- [ ] Say how the container stops: with `--rm`, it is removed by itself when the render finishes.
      If your `README` also uses `docker compose up -d`, add `docker compose down` to stop and remove it.
- [ ] Link to your `CONTRIBUTING.md` for anyone who wants to change the project.
:::

**Your `CONTRIBUTING.md`:** use the [example `CONTRIBUTING.md`](https://github.com/UBC-MDS/DSCI_522_project-template-breast-cancer-predictor/blob/1.0.0/CONTRIBUTING.md) as your template.
It replaces any setup steps from Milestone 1 (such as installing packages on your own computer).

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## What your `CONTRIBUTING.md` must include

- [ ] Link to your `README` for the setup steps (ssh key, `docker compose pull`), instead of repeating them.
- [ ] Work in the container with Positron over ssh: write the steps from the [step-by-step guide in part 1](#positron-ssh) for your project
      (the steps the `README` already covers can be a link), including installing Positron, the Git name and email check, which interpreter to pick, and the fixes for when it doesn't connect.
- [ ] Add or update a package: on a branch, add it with your environment manager, commit and push.
      Wait for GitHub Actions to publish the new image and update the tag in `docker-compose.yml`,
      then run `git pull` and `docker compose pull`.
- [ ] Publish the report: after re-rendering, copy it to `docs/index.html` and push (see [part 3](#publish-your-report-on-github-pages)).
:::

::: callout-important
## Reproducibility is worth 20 points

We launch your container and run your analysis by following your `README` **exactly as written**.
The less of it we can run (a missing package, a wrong file path, a step we had to guess or fix), the more points you lose.
Test them on **both Windows and Mac**.
If your team doesn't have both, ask another team to test them.
:::

### 3. Publish your report on GitHub Pages

Anyone should be able to read your report online without cloning your repository.
You publish it by hand: put a [self-contained]{.term tabindex="0" data-tip="A self-contained HTML file has everything it needs (figures, styling, scripts) packed inside the one file, instead of in separate files next to it. So it still works after you copy it somewhere else."} copy of your rendered report at `docs/index.html`.
If you already published your report in Milestone 1, switch to this setup anyway, because later milestones build on it.

1.  Make the rendered report one self-contained HTML file, in its YAML header
    (skip this if your `_quarto.yml` already sets it):

    ```yaml
    format:
      html:
        embed-resources: true
    ```

    If you have only been rendering to PDF, render to HTML as well.

2.  Render your report, then copy it into `docs/` as `index.html`, and add an empty `.nojekyll` file:

    ```bash
    mkdir -p docs
    cp <path-to-your-report>.html docs/index.html
    touch docs/.nojekyll
    ```

    ::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
    ## If you also render a PDF: fix the "Other Formats" link

    When you render more than one format, Quarto adds a link to the others
    (for example "Typst") under **Other Formats** in the HTML report.
    That link points to a file next to the report, which is not in `docs/`,
    so on GitHub Pages it gives a 404.
    Either remove the link, in your report's YAML header or your `_quarto.yml`:

    ```yaml
    format:
      html:
        format-links: false
    ```

    or point it to the PDF in your repository:

    ```yaml
    format:
      html:
        format-links:
          - html   # stops Quarto adding its own link
          - text: PDF
            href: https://github.com/ubc-mds-2026-27/<your-repository>/blob/main/<path-to-your-report>.pdf
            icon: file-pdf
    ```
    :::

3.  Commit and push `docs/`.
    Check that your `.gitignore` does not ignore `docs/` or `.html` files.

4.  On GitHub.com, go to **Settings \> Pages** \> **Deploy from a branch**,
    choose the `main` branch and the `/docs` folder, and click **Save**.

5.  After a few minutes, open `https://ubc-mds-2026-27.github.io/<your-repository>/`
    and check that the whole report shows, including its figures.

6.  Put this URL in your `README` (as the link to your rendered report)
    and in the **About** section of your repository.

::: callout-important
## Keep the published report up to date

`docs/index.html` is a copy.
Each time you re-render your report, copy it into `docs/` again and push.
We grade from your `1.0.0` release, and the report on GitHub Pages should match it.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Why this works

-   GitHub Pages can publish the files in a `docs/` folder on `main`, exactly as they are.
-   When someone visits your site's address, the server shows the file named `index.html`.
-   With `embed-resources: true`, the report is one HTML file that holds its figures and styling,
    so it still works after you copy it.
-   `.nojekyll` tells GitHub Pages to serve your file as it is
    (see [Turning off Jekyll with `.nojekyll`](https://ubc-mds.github.io/DSCI_521_platforms-dsci_book/lectures/quarto-github-pages.html#nojekyll)).

Copying by hand is easy to forget, so it is not how you would publish a larger site.
In DSCI 524 you will use tools that build and publish a website for you.
:::

## Submission instructions

1.  Just before you submit, after your last commit, create a GitHub release named exactly `1.0.0`
    ([how to create a release](https://docs.github.com/en/repositories/releasing-projects-on-github/managing-releases-in-a-repository#creating-a-release)).
    It records the state of your repository at submission, so you can keep working on the next milestone.
2.  On Gradescope, enter these four URLs (there is no PDF to make):
    -   the GitHub release: the link ending in `/releases/tag/1.0.0`, not `/releases/latest` (which changes at your next release)
    -   your group project's repository (general one without GitHub release)
    -   your report on GitHub Pages
    -   your image on Docker Hub

You don't need to include Milestone 1 feedback in this submission.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Check yourself before submitting

- [ ] The GitHub Actions run succeeded, and the Docker Hub tag lists `linux/amd64` and `linux/arm64`
- [ ] `docker-compose.yml` uses your **newest** `sha-` tag on Docker Hub, not `latest` or an older one (`git pull` after the last workflow run)
- [ ] (Python) `pyproject.toml` pins every package with `==` and lists `ipykernel`, `nbclient` and `pyyaml`
- [ ] (R) `DESCRIPTION` pins every package and lists `knitr` and `rmarkdown`
- [ ] Someone on Windows and someone on Mac cloned your repository fresh, followed your `README` steps exactly, and rendered the report without changing any file
- [ ] Your repository is public, in the `UBC-MDS-2026-27` organization, with a name that describes your project
- [ ] No unnecessary files are committed (such as `.venv/`, `renv/library/`, `.DS_Store`, or `_files/` folders): your `.gitignore` covers them
- [ ] Your `CONTRIBUTING.md` says how to work in the container, add a package and republish the report, and your `README` doesn't
- [ ] Your report on GitHub Pages shows in full, with its figures, and matches your release
- [ ] The GitHub Pages URL is in your `README` and in the repository's **About** section
- [ ] You created the `1.0.0` release
:::

::: callout-important
## Teamwork expectations (these are marked)

-   **Everyone contributes equally** to code, writing and project management,
    shown by a roughly equal number of commits, pull request reviews and GitHub issue comments.
-   Use the [GitHub flow](https://docs.github.com/en/get-started/using-github/github-flow):
    a small branch for each feature or fix, in your team's repository (not a fork),
    with a name that says what it does (`add-dockerfile`, not `branch1`).
    Every change goes through a pull request, reviewed by at least one teammate before it is merged.
-   Commit and push every time you work on the project, with meaningful commit messages
    (one or two less meaningful ones are OK).
-   Talk to your teammates in GitHub issues, not email or Slack:
    at least 3 issues per person on average in this milestone.
-   Your question, analysis and visualization should make sense. They don't have to be complicated.
-   Write your `README` in full sentences with proper grammar. Keep point form under 10% of it.
:::
